why.correct: Meiosis I separates the homologs, so each daughter cell gets 23 chromosomes, one from each pair. The sister chromatids are still joined until anaphase II. A haploid cell with double chromosomes has finished meiosis I but not meiosis II.
options: A cell in G1 before meiosis is diploid, with 46 single chromosomes, not 23 double ones.
After meiosis II each cell has 23 single chromosomes; the sister chromatids have already separated.
Correct. 23 double chromosomes is the state after meiosis I and before the sisters separate in meiosis II.
A cell in metaphase of mitosis has all 46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids.

why.correct: In anaphase I, the homologs move apart but each is still two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. No chromatids split, so the count stays at 46 chromosomes (92 chromatids), 23 moving to each end.
options: 23 is the number that ends up at each end, or in each cell after telophase I, not the total in the cell during anaphase I.
Correct. 46 double chromosomes: the homologs separate but the sisters do not.
92 is the count in anaphase of mitosis, when sister chromatids split and each becomes a chromosome. In anaphase I they stay joined.
69 would be one and a half sets, which never occurs in a normal division.

why.correct: Pairing, crossing over and lining up in pairs are unique to meiosis I. Sister chromatids separate in mitosis and meiosis II, both divisions use a spindle, and both are preceded by one round of DNA copying.
options: Correct. Homologs pair only in prophase I of meiosis.
Correct. Crossing over needs paired homologs, so it happens only in prophase I.
Correct. In metaphase I the chromosomes line up as pairs; in mitosis they line up singly.
Sister chromatids separate in mitosis and in meiosis II, not in meiosis I.
Every division, mitosis and both divisions of meiosis, uses a spindle.
DNA is copied once before mitosis and once before meiosis, so this does not tell them apart.

why.correct: Prophase I pairs the homologs and lets them cross over; metaphase I lines them up as pairs; anaphase I separates the homologs; telophase I gives two haploid cells with double chromosomes. Meiosis II then separates the sister chromatids, giving four haploid cells with single chromosomes.
Anaphase I comes between metaphase I and telophase I. In it, the homologs of each pair are pulled to opposite ends while each keeps its two sister chromatids.
options: Anaphase II belongs to the second division, after telophase I.
Metaphase II also belongs to the second division, after telophase I.
DNA is copied once, before meiosis starts, not between metaphase I and telophase I.
Correct. Anaphase I separates the homologs.

why.correct: Anaphase I separates the homologs, not the sister chromatids. The sisters stay joined at the centromere until anaphase II. That is why each cell after meiosis I has 23 chromosomes that are still double.
options: This step is right. Pairing of homologs is the hallmark of prophase I.
This step is right. Crossing over happens while the homologs are paired.
This step is right. In metaphase I, chromosomes line up as pairs.
This is the error. Anaphase I separates homologs; sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
This step is right. Each cell gets one member of each of the 23 pairs.

why.correct: Meiosis I is the reduction division. It halves the number of chromosomes and chromatids and the DNA in each cell, but each chromosome stays double until meiosis II.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in the cell
variables.why: Meiosis I sends one homolog of each pair to each cell, so the count falls from 46 to 23.

variables.name: Number of chromatids in the cell
variables.why: Each of the 23 chromosomes still has two chromatids, so the cell has 46 chromatids instead of 92.

variables.name: Chromatids per chromosome
variables.why: Sister chromatids stay joined through meiosis I, so each chromosome is still made of two chromatids.

variables.name: Amount of DNA in the cell
variables.why: Half the chromatids went to the other cell, so each cell has half the DNA: back to the amount of a G1 body cell.

why.correct: In a man's meiosis, the X and the Y behave as a homologous pair and separate in anaphase I. A sperm carrying both an X and a Y means that pair failed to separate: nondisjunction in meiosis I.
options: Correct. The X and Y are homologs, and homologs separate in meiosis I.
In meiosis II, sister chromatids separate. A failure there would give a sperm with two X chromosomes or two Y chromosomes, not one of each.
The mother gave only her normal single X. The extra chromosome came from the father.
An error after the egg and sperm joined could not supply a Y from the father alongside his X, and it would usually give a mix of cell lines rather than XXY in every cell.

why.correct: Two identical copies are sister chromatids that failed to separate. Sisters separate in anaphase II, so the error was in meiosis II. If the homologs had failed to separate in meiosis I, the oocyte would carry one copy from each of the mother's two chromosome 21s, which differ.
options: Nondisjunction in meiosis I sends both homologs to one cell. Homologs differ in their alleles, so the two copies would not be identical.
Correct. Identical copies point to sister chromatids that stayed together in meiosis II.
An error in an earlier mitosis would give a stem cell with an extra chromosome whose copies then pair in meiosis, not simply two identical copies in the oocyte.
Copying DNA makes the sister chromatids in every cell. Copying itself does not put an extra chromosome into a gamete.

why.correct: 2n = 12 means 6 pairs. Each pair can send either homolog to a gamete, and the pairs assort independently: 2⁶ = 64.
options: Correct. 6 pairs, 2 choices each: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64.
12 is the diploid number, not the number of combinations.
24 is 2 × 12. The choices for each pair multiply; they are not added or doubled once.
4,096 is 2¹², which treats all 12 chromosomes as independent choices. Only the 6 pairs are; one member of each pair goes to each gamete.

why.correct: Every egg carries an X, because a woman's cells have two X chromosomes and no Y. A man's X and Y separate in meiosis I, so half his sperm carry an X and half a Y. The sperm that joins the egg decides: X gives XX, Y gives XY.
options: An egg never carries a Y chromosome; a woman has none to give.
Each parent does give one sex chromosome, but the mother's is always an X, so only the father's contribution varies.
Correct. The sperm carries either an X or a Y; the egg always carries an X.
The chromosomes present at the start, and SRY on the Y, set whether the gonad becomes a testis. Hormones follow from that.

why.correct: SRY is the switch that makes the early gonad become a testis. If crossing over in the father's meiosis moved SRY onto an X, an XX child develops testes and a male body. Other Y genes needed for making sperm are missing, which explains the infertility.
options: Testosterone is a steroid made from cholesterol by enzymes, not a gene product copied from the Y. The testis makes it once SRY has made the gonad a testis.
An autosome is not Y DNA, and an extra autosome would not produce testes.
Genes for making sperm would not create testes; the gonad must first become a testis, which is SRY's job.
Correct. SRY alone is enough to turn the early gonad into a testis.

why.correct: Homologous chromosomes are the two members of a pair, one inherited from each parent: same genes in the same order, but possibly different alleles. Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of one chromosome made in S phase and joined at the centromere.
options: Correct. Homologs are a matched pair from two parents; sisters are copies of one chromosome.
This reverses the two. Sister chromatids are the identical copies.
Homologs carry the same genes, often in different versions (alleles).
Body cells hold homologous pairs, and every cell that copies its DNA has sister chromatids. Gametes have no homologous pairs.

why.correct: The two identical halves of one copied chromosome, joined at the centromere, are sister chromatids.
options: Correct. These are the two copies of one chromosome.
Homologous chromosomes are the two different chromosomes of a pair, one from each parent, shown in different shading.
The centromere is the narrow joint where the sisters are held, not the two arms.
Kinetochores are protein structures on the centromere where spindle microtubules attach.

why.correct: The two chromosomes of a matching pair, one from each parent, same length and same genes, are homologous chromosomes.
options: Sister chromatids are identical copies joined at one centromere, not two separate chromosomes from two parents.
Correct. The two members of a pair are homologous chromosomes.
A gamete is a whole cell, not a chromosome.
Chiasmata are the crossing points between paired homologs in prophase I. This drawing shows no crossing over.

why.correct: Skin cells are diploid, so 2n = 78. Sperm are haploid: n = 78 ÷ 2 = 39.
options: 78 is the diploid number. A gamete with 78 would give offspring with 156.
156 doubles instead of halving.
Correct. Gametes carry one member of each of the 39 pairs.
A chromosome cannot be split in half. Meiosis halves the number of whole chromosomes, from 39 pairs to one of each.

why.correct: The error in meiosis I puts both homologs into one cell and neither into the other. Meiosis II then splits each cell's chromosomes normally: the first cell gives two gametes with 24 chromosomes, and the second gives two with 22. All four are abnormal.
options: An error that puts both homologs into one cell must change the count in that cell's products and in its partner's.
One abnormal gamete cannot arise, because an extra chromosome in one cell always means a missing one in another.
Two of four abnormal is the result of an error in meiosis II in one of the two cells: one gamete with 24, one with 22 and two normal.
Correct. Meiosis I nondisjunction makes every gamete from that cell abnormal: two with 24 and two with 22.

why.correct: The female gamete is the oocyte. It completes its last division only after a sperm enters it; the finished cell is an ovum.
options: Ovum is the name for the egg after it has finished meiosis.
Sperm is the male gamete.
Correct. Oocyte (oo- = egg, -cyte = cell) is the female gamete.
A gonad is the organ that makes gametes (a testis or an ovary), not the gamete itself.

why.correct: Meiosis in the ovary begins before birth and pauses until shortly before an oocyte is released. The proteins that hold homologs and sister chromatids together are not replaced during that pause, so after 40 years chromosomes are more likely to separate early or go to the wrong end: nondisjunction.
options: Oocytes are not produced by continuing stem cell division in adult women; they are all formed before birth. Age-related mutations explain little of the chromosome-number risk.
Correct. Long storage weakens the cohesion proteins, making nondisjunction more likely.
Meiosis II is not skipped with age, and skipping it would give gametes with double the DNA, not the pattern seen.
Older oocytes do have less healthy mitochondria, but the main, best-supported cause of chromosome errors is loss of the proteins that hold chromosomes together.

why.correct: Crossing over swaps matching pieces between homologs in prophase I, so a chromosome in a gamete can be part grandmother's, part grandfather's: a new combination of alleles on one chromosome.
options: Independent assortment mixes whole chromosomes: which homolog of each pair goes into a gamete. It does not change what is on any one chromosome.
Correct. Crossing over recombines alleles within a chromosome.
Nondisjunction changes the number of chromosomes, not their combinations of alleles, and it is an error, not a routine source of variety.
Replication makes identical copies; it does not mix the two parents' alleles.

why.correct: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules, mature and are stored in the epididymis, travel the ductus deferens up through the inguinal canal and behind the bladder, enter the ejaculatory duct inside the prostate, and pass through the prostatic, membranous and spongy parts of the urethra to the outside.
From the rete testis, efferent ductules carry sperm into the head of the epididymis. They travel through its body and tail, then into the ductus deferens.
options: The seminal vesicle adds fluid at the start of the ejaculatory duct; sperm do not pass through it.
Correct. The epididymis lies between the testis and the ductus deferens.
The bulbourethral glands empty into the spongy urethra; sperm do not pass through them.
The inguinal canal is a passage in the abdominal wall that the spermatic cord runs through, not a duct between the testis and the ductus deferens.

why.correct: Interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells, sit in the connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules. LH from the anterior pituitary drives them to make testosterone.
options: The epididymis lining helps sperm mature; it does not make testosterone.
Correct. Leydig cells between the tubules are the testis's endocrine cells.
The dartos is smooth muscle in the scrotal wall that wrinkles the skin in cold.
The tunica albuginea is the tough connective tissue capsule of the testis.

why.correct: The dartos is smooth muscle under the scrotal skin; it contracts in cold and wrinkles the skin, reducing heat loss. The cremaster is skeletal muscle around each testis and its cord; it contracts and pulls the testes toward the warm body.
options: Correct. Dartos: wrinkling. Cremaster: lifting.
This reverses the two muscles.
The bulbospongiosus is at the root of the penis and drives expulsion of semen. It does not act on the scrotum.
The detrusor is the bladder wall muscle and the external urethral sphincter surrounds the urethra; neither acts on the scrotum.

why.correct: The plexus is a mesh of veins wound around the testicular artery. Blood returning from the cool scrotum takes up heat from the warm arterial blood flowing the other way, so arterial blood is already cooler when it reaches the testis: countercurrent heat exchange.
options: Correct. Heat passes from the artery to the surrounding veins.
The plexus is a set of veins; it releases no hormone.
The plexus lies deep in the spermatic cord, not in the skin, and it is made of veins, not glands.
Blood keeps flowing through the plexus. Cooling comes from heat exchange between opposite streams, not from blood standing still.

why.correct: The cut ducts stop sperm from reaching the urethra. Most of the semen comes from the seminal vesicles and prostate, downstream of the cut, so volume barely changes. Testosterone leaves the testis in the blood, not through the ducts, so it is unaffected.
options: Sperm are only a few percent of semen volume, and testosterone travels in the blood, not the ductus deferens.
The accessory glands still make and release their fluids, and nothing in the operation raises testosterone.
The seminal vesicles, which supply the fructose and most of the volume, still empty into the ejaculatory ducts. It is the sperm that are missing.
Correct. Sperm are blocked; gland fluid and blood-borne testosterone are not.

why.correct: The seminal vesicles supply about 60 to 70% of semen volume: alkaline fluid with fructose, prostaglandins and a clotting protein.
options: The prostate supplies about 20 to 30%, less than the seminal vesicles.
The bulbourethral glands add only a small amount of mucus before ejaculation.
Correct. The seminal vesicles contribute the largest share.
The epididymis stores sperm; it is part of the duct system, not an accessory gland, and adds little volume.

why.correct: The prostate wraps around the first part of the urethra just below the bladder. As it enlarges with age (benign prostatic hyperplasia), it squeezes the prostatic urethra and slows the outflow of urine.
options: The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder and do not surround the urethra.
The bulbourethral glands are pea-sized glands in the pelvic floor; their enlargement is rare and not the cause of this common pattern.
The epididymis is on the back of the testis, far from the urinary outflow.
Correct. An enlarged prostate narrows the urethra it surrounds.

why.correct: The seminal vesicles add a protein that clots semen into a gel as soon as it is ejaculated. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA), an enzyme from the prostate, breaks that gel down over 15 to 30 minutes, freeing the sperm to swim.
options: Correct. Seminal vesicle protein clots; prostate PSA liquefies.
This reverses the roles of the two glands.
Bulbourethral mucus is released before ejaculation as a lubricant. It does not form the clot.
Fructose is a sugar sperm use for energy; it does not form a gel.

why.correct: The single corpus spongiosum runs along the underside of the penis around the spongy urethra and widens at its end into the glans.
options: The two corpora cavernosa lie on the upper side and do not contain the urethra.
The tunica albuginea is the capsule around each column, not an erectile column.
The prepuce is the fold of skin over the glans.
Correct. The corpus spongiosum holds the urethra and forms the glans.

why.correct: The corpora cavernosa have a thick tunica albuginea that squeezes their draining veins shut, so pressure inside rises close to arterial pressure. The corpus spongiosum's capsule is thin, so its pressure stays lower. Its softness keeps the urethra inside it open for semen to pass.
options: The corpus spongiosum fills with blood too; it has its own arteries.
Correct. A thin capsule traps less blood, so the tissue stays compressible and the urethra stays open.
The corpus spongiosum is erectile tissue with smooth muscle, like the other two columns.
Sympathetic activity ends an erection in all three columns; it does not keep one soft during it.

why.correct: Cyclic GMP makes the smooth muscle relax, not contract. Relaxed arterial walls and relaxed walls around the blood spaces are what let blood rush in.
options: This step is right. Sacral parasympathetic neurons (S2–S4) start the erection.
This step is right. Nitric oxide is the messenger that reaches the smooth muscle.
This is the error. cGMP relaxes smooth muscle; contraction would end the erection.
This step is right. Vasodilation raises inflow.
This step is right. Compressed veins cut outflow, trapping blood.

why.correct: Nitroglycerin releases nitric oxide, which raises cGMP in vascular smooth muscle. Sildenafil blocks PDE5, the enzyme that breaks cGMP down. Together they relax vessels throughout the body, and blood pressure can fall dangerously.
options: Correct. More cGMP made and less broken down: widespread vasodilation.
Sildenafil does not block nitroglycerin; it strengthens its effect.
Both drugs widen vessels, not narrow them.
Nitroglycerin supplies nitric oxide; it does not block it.

why.correct: Emission is driven by sympathetic neurons from about T10–L2. Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins contracts the smooth muscle of the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate, and closes the bladder neck.
options: Parasympathetic nerves produce erection, not emission.
Somatic motor neurons in the pudendal nerve drive expulsion, the next phase, through skeletal muscle.
The gut's own nerve network does not control the reproductive ducts.
Correct. Sympathetic nerves contract the smooth muscle of the ducts and glands.

why.correct: During emission, norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins contracts the internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck. With those receptor proteins blocked, the neck stays open, and when the pelvic muscles contract, semen takes the easier path back into the bladder: retrograde ejaculation. It leaves with the next urine, which is cloudy and holds sperm. (These drugs can also weaken emission itself, so less semen is made to move; then the urine holds no extra sperm.)
options: Sperm production depends on hormones, not on alpha-1 receptor proteins in the bladder neck, and the sperm in his urine show they are still being made.
Correct. An open bladder neck lets semen flow backward into the bladder.
The pudendal nerve is somatic and uses acetylcholine at skeletal muscle; an alpha-1 blocker does not block it.
The sperm-filled urine shows semen was produced and moved, but went the wrong way.

why.correct: The spermatic cord holds the ductus deferens, the testicular artery, the pampiniform plexus of veins, nerves and lymphatic vessels, wrapped in connective tissue and strands of cremaster muscle. The ejaculatory duct and seminal vesicle lie deep in the pelvis.
options: Correct. The ductus deferens climbs from the scrotum in the cord.
Correct. The testicular artery reaches the testis through the cord.
Correct. The veins of the plexus drain the testis through the cord.
The ejaculatory duct lies inside the prostate, far below the inguinal canal.
The seminal vesicles sit behind the bladder in the pelvis.
Correct. Cremaster fibers wrap the cord and the testis.

why.correct: The inguinal canal is a short, slanting passage through the muscles of the lower abdominal wall. The testis came down through it before birth, and the spermatic cord runs through it.
options: The femoral canal lies below the groin ligament, beside the femoral vein, and does not carry the cord.
The obturator foramen is a large opening in the hip bone, mostly closed by membrane; the cord does not pass through it.
Correct. The cord runs in the inguinal canal.
No passage by that name carries the cord.

why.correct: The coiled, pouch-like gland on the back of the bladder is a seminal vesicle.
options: Correct. The seminal vesicle sits behind the bladder, above the prostate.
The prostate lies below the bladder, around the urethra.
The bulbourethral gland is a small round gland below the prostate.
The epididymis lies on the back of the testis, in the scrotum.

why.correct: The gland directly below the bladder, wrapped around the first part of the urethra, is the prostate.
options: The bladder is the hollow organ above it.
The seminal vesicle lies behind the bladder, higher up.
The bulbourethral gland is smaller and lies below the prostate.
Correct. The prostate surrounds the prostatic urethra.

why.correct: The network of channels at the back of the testis, where the tubules drain, is the rete testis.
options: The efferent ductules leave the rete and carry sperm into the epididymis.
Correct. The rete testis collects sperm from the seminiferous tubules.
The tunica albuginea is the white capsule around the testis.
The head of the epididymis sits on top of the testis, beyond the efferent ductules.

why.correct: The two large columns of erectile tissue on the upper side of the penis are the corpora cavernosa.
options: The corpus spongiosum is the single smaller column below, around the urethra.
Correct. The two dorsal columns are the corpora cavernosa.
The cavernosal arteries run inside the corpora cavernosa; they are the small vessels at their centers.
The spongy urethra runs through the corpus spongiosum.

why.correct: The strands of skeletal muscle wrapping each testis are the cremaster muscles; they lift the testes in the cold.
options: The dartos is a thin sheet of smooth muscle just under the skin.
Correct. The cremaster muscles surround the testes and their cords.
The detrusor is the muscle of the bladder wall.
The scrotal septum is the midline wall between the two compartments.

why.correct: Spermatogonia divide by mitosis; a committed one becomes a primary spermatocyte, which completes meiosis I to give two secondary spermatocytes. Meiosis II gives four spermatids, and spermiogenesis reshapes each into a sperm.
Meiosis I halves the chromosome number but leaves the sister chromatids joined, so a secondary spermatocyte has 23 double chromosomes.
options: Spermatogonia are diploid stem cells with 46 chromosomes.
A primary spermatocyte is diploid: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids.
Correct. Haploid with double chromosomes: the stage between meiosis I and meiosis II.
A spermatid has finished meiosis II, so its 23 chromosomes are single.

why.correct: Each primary spermatocyte gives two secondary spermatocytes, each of which gives two spermatids: 4 per primary spermatocyte. Spermiogenesis reshapes without dividing. 50 × 4 = 200 sperm.
options: Spermiogenesis does not divide cells, but meiosis does, twice.
100 counts only one division. Meiosis has two.
Correct. Four sperm from each primary spermatocyte.
400 would need a third division. Spermiogenesis only reshapes.

why.correct: Spermiogenesis is the reshaping of a round spermatid into a sperm: the DNA packs, the acrosome and tail form, and excess cytoplasm is shed. No division happens.
options: Correct. Spermiogenesis reshapes spermatids into sperm.
Mitosis happens in the spermatogonia, at the start of the process, not after meiosis.
Meiosis I came before, making the secondary spermatocytes.
The spermatogonium is the stem cell at the start of the line, not a step after the spermatid.

why.correct: Androgen-binding protein holds testosterone in the tubule fluid, keeping its concentration there many times the blood level. Spermatogenesis needs that high local level.
options: Testosterone reaches muscles through the blood bound to plasma proteins; androgen-binding protein works inside the tubules.
DHT is made by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase in target tissues, not by a binding protein.
Blood testosterone still reaches the hypothalamus and pituitary; the binding protein acts locally in the testis.
Correct. It traps testosterone where the germ cells are.

why.correct: Self-tolerance was established in childhood, before meiosis began. Spermatocytes and spermatids make new surface proteins that white blood cells have never been taught to ignore, so they would be attacked as foreign. The Sertoli tight junctions keep antibodies and lymphocytes away from them.
options: Spermatogonia need nutrients too; they get them directly from the blood side of the barrier.
Correct. The barrier shields cells whose proteins look foreign to the immune system.
Spermatogonia are diploid, not haploid.
Sperm are released into the lumen on the far side of the barrier; the barrier does not hold them back.

why.correct: The tail moves by motor proteins that use ATP. The ATP comes from the spiral of mitochondria in the midpiece. Of the parts listed, only the midpiece mitochondria supply the energy for swimming. (A fault in the tail's own motor proteins, which look normal under a light microscope, can also stop sperm from swimming.)
options: The acrosome holds enzymes used at the egg; it does not power swimming.
Correct. The midpiece mitochondria make the ATP that drives the flagellum.
The nucleus carries the DNA; it does not move the sperm.
The membrane over the head matters when the sperm meets the egg, not for swimming.

why.correct: The acrosome is a cap-like sac of digestive enzymes over the front of the head, made from the Golgi apparatus. The enzymes let the sperm digest a path through the layers around the egg.
options: Mitochondria are in the midpiece.
The microtubules are in the flagellum, the tail.
The chromosomes are in the nucleus, behind the acrosome.
Correct. The acrosome is an enzyme-filled cap.

why.correct: The cap over the front of the sperm head is the acrosome, a sac of digestive enzymes.
options: The nucleus fills the head beneath the cap.
Correct. This cap is the acrosome.
The centriole sits at the base of the head, where the tail begins.
The midpiece is behind the head, packed with mitochondria.

why.correct: The short region just behind the head, wrapped in a spiral of mitochondria, is the midpiece.
options: The head holds the nucleus and acrosome.
Correct. The midpiece holds the mitochondria.
The tail is the long whip-like part beyond the midpiece.
The end piece is the thin tip of the tail.

why.correct: The tall supporting cell in the tubule wall that FSH acts on is the Sertoli (sustentacular) cell. It releases androgen-binding protein and inhibin.
options: Leydig cells lie in the spaces between the tubules and respond to LH.
Correct. The Sertoli cell sits inside the tubule wall.
A spermatogonium is a stem cell on the basement membrane; FSH's main target here is the supporting cell.
Red blood cells are in the capillaries, not in the tubule wall.

why.correct: LH binds receptor proteins on the Leydig (interstitial) cells and drives them to make testosterone.
options: Correct. LH drives testosterone production by the Leydig cells.
FSH acts mainly on the Sertoli cells.
Inhibin comes from the Sertoli cells and acts on the pituitary.
GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary, not on the testis.

why.correct: When the gonad fails, its products fall and the feedback brakes lift. The hypothalamus and pituitary push harder, so GnRH, LH and FSH rise, but the damaged testis cannot respond. Low testosterone with high LH and FSH is the pattern of testicular (primary) failure.

variables.name: Blood testosterone
variables.why: The Leydig cells that make testosterone no longer work, so blood testosterone falls.

variables.name: Inhibin
variables.why: Inhibin comes from the Sertoli cells, which have stopped working.

variables.name: GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus
variables.why: With little testosterone, the brake on the hypothalamus is lifted, so it releases more GnRH.

variables.name: LH
variables.why: Less testosterone braking the pituitary, and more GnRH driving it, raise LH.

variables.name: FSH
variables.why: Both brakes on FSH, testosterone and inhibin, are gone, so FSH rises, usually even more than LH.

variables.name: Sperm count
variables.why: Without working Sertoli cells and a high local testosterone level, spermatogenesis stops.

why.correct: Loss of the pituitary gonadotropins removes the drive to the testes. Testosterone, sperm output and testis size fall together, and GnRH rises because the feedback brake has lifted. Low testosterone with low LH points to a problem above the testis.

variables.name: LH
variables.why: The cells that make LH are gone.

variables.name: Blood testosterone
variables.why: Without LH, the Leydig cells receive no signal to make testosterone.

variables.name: GnRH release
variables.why: Low testosterone lifts the brake on the hypothalamus, so it releases more GnRH, but the pituitary cannot respond.

variables.name: Sperm count
variables.why: Without FSH and without the high local testosterone that LH normally drives, spermatogenesis fails.

variables.name: Size of the testes
variables.why: Without gonadotropin drive, the tubules and Leydig cells shrink.

why.correct: The injected androgen brakes the hypothalamus and pituitary, so GnRH, LH and FSH fall. Without LH, his Leydig cells stop making testosterone, and the very high local level inside the tubules is lost, along with FSH support. Spermatogenesis needs that local level, which blood testosterone from injections cannot reach. His testes also shrink. You can follow the same chain in the endocrine chapter's anabolic steroid scenario.
options: Testosterone is needed for spermatogenesis; it does not kill sperm.
Correct. Suppressed LH and FSH remove the local drive to sperm production.
Hormone injections do not block a duct; the problem is that few sperm are made.
Cells do not convert from one type to the other; both types simply lose their pituitary drive.

why.correct: Chemotherapy kills rapidly dividing germ cells but usually spares the Leydig cells, so testosterone and LH stay normal. Sertoli cells supporting few germ cells release less inhibin, so the brake on FSH weakens and FSH rises on its own.
options: GnRH comes from the hypothalamus, not the pituitary, and more GnRH would raise LH as well as FSH.
If Leydig cells were destroyed, testosterone would be low and LH high.
Broken receptor proteins would raise both testosterone and LH, because feedback would fail too.
Correct. Low inhibin selectively raises FSH.

why.correct: Inhibin comes from the Sertoli cells, not the Leydig cells. It acts on the anterior pituitary to lower FSH release.
options: This step is right. GnRH is released in bursts every 1 to 3 hours.
This step is right. GnRH is the releasing hormone for both gonadotropins.
This step is right. LH targets the Leydig cells.
This step is right. The Sertoli cells respond to both.
This is the error. Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells, make inhibin.

why.correct: The pituitary responds to GnRH arriving in pulses. Under steady, unchanging GnRH signaling, its cells stop responding, so LH (and FSH) release falls after a brief rise. Without LH, the Leydig cells make little testosterone, which slows the growth of androgen-sensitive prostate cancer.
options: The Leydig cells are intact; they simply lose their LH signal.
Correct. Continuous GnRH shuts down LH release.
The drug acts on the pituitary; blocking androgen receptor proteins would not lower testosterone, and would usually raise it.
Aromatase makes estradiol from testosterone regardless of GnRH, and it would not account for such low testosterone.

why.correct: Testosterone enlarges the larynx, builds muscle, starts spermatogenesis and, through DHT in hair follicles, grows facial hair. Plate closure depends on estradiol made from testosterone by aromatase, so testosterone does not close the plates by itself.
options: Correct. Testosterone enlarges the larynx and lengthens the vocal cords.
Correct. Testosterone speeds protein synthesis in skeletal muscle.
Correct. Spermatogenesis needs a high local testosterone level.
Correct. DHT acting on hair follicles drives male-pattern hair growth.
The plates close under estrogen. Men who cannot make or respond to estrogen keep growing into adulthood.

why.correct: In androgen insensitivity, testosterone is made normally, even in excess, but the androgen receptor protein does not work. The male external genitals never form, the brain's feedback brake fails so LH and testosterone run high, and aromatase turns the extra testosterone into estrogen, which develops breasts.
options: Her testosterone is high, so her testes clearly make it.
She has testes, so SRY did its job; SRY is what makes the gonad a testis.
Without LH, testosterone would be low, not high.
Correct. The hormone is present, but cells cannot respond to it.

why.correct: Testosterone stimulates erythropoietin release and red cell production in the bone marrow, so men carry a higher proportion of red cells in their blood.
options: The testes do not cause blood loss.
Estrogen does not destroy red blood cells.
Correct. Testosterone promotes red blood cell production.
More plasma would lower the hematocrit, not raise it.

why.correct: The fimbriae are the finger-like fringes at the open end of each uterine tube. They drape over the ovary and sweep a released oocyte into the tube.
options: Correct. The fringed projections at the end of the tube are the fimbriae.
The ovarian ligament is a cord running from the ovary to the side of the uterus, not a fringe at the end of the tube.
The broad ligament is a wide sheet of peritoneum draped over the uterus, tubes and ovaries, not a set of finger-like projections.
The ampulla is the wide middle part of the tube, farther in from the fringed opening.

why.correct: The broad ligament is a wide double fold of peritoneum draped over the uterus, uterine tubes and ovaries, anchoring them loosely to the pelvic side walls.
options: The suspensory ligament of the ovary is a narrow fold from the ovary to the pelvic wall that carries the ovarian vessels, not the wide sheet across the uterus.
The perimetrium is the serous layer covering the uterus itself. The broad ligament is the fold that continues out from it to the pelvic walls.
Correct. The wide sheet of peritoneum is the broad ligament.
The round ligaments are cords that run forward from the uterus to the groin.

why.correct: The cervix is the narrow lower end of the uterus that projects into the top of the vagina, with a canal running through it.
options: The fundus is the rounded top of the uterus, above where the tubes enter.
Correct. The narrow neck at the bottom of the uterus is the cervix.
The body is the main central part of the uterus, above the cervix.
The isthmus is the narrow part of the uterine tube next to the uterus, not the lower end of the uterus.

why.correct: The functional layer is the thick inner part of the endometrium facing the cavity. It breaks down and is shed at menstruation, then is rebuilt from the basal layer.
options: The perimetrium is the outer serous covering and is never shed.
The myometrium is the smooth muscle layer. It contracts during a period but is not shed.
The basal layer stays in place. It is the source of the cells that regrow the functional layer.
Correct. Only the functional layer is shed.

why.correct: The basal layer supplies the cells that rebuild the functional layer each month. Without it, little functional layer grows, so there is little to shed and periods become scant or stop, even though her hormones are normal.
options: Correct. No basal layer means no regrowth, so little or nothing is shed.
Exposed, scarred muscle does not build a lining to shed, so flow falls rather than rises.
Only the functional layer is shed, but it has to be regrown from the basal layer first. With the basal layer gone, there is nothing to rebuild it.
Scraping the uterus does not affect the ovaries; her hormone cycle continues. Her periods change because the lining cannot regrow.

why.correct: The ampulla is the long, wide middle part of the tube. It is where sperm usually reach the oocyte.
options: The isthmus is the narrow part near the uterus; the oocyte usually passes it later.
Correct. The ampulla is the usual meeting place.
The part within the uterine wall is the last, shortest segment, which the oocyte reaches only days later.
The fimbriae catch the oocyte but are outside the tube proper.

why.correct: The reproductive tract is a continuous passage: vagina, cervical canal, uterine cavity, uterine tube, and then the tube's open end into the peritoneal cavity. Bacteria can climb that path and reach the peritoneum.
options: Correct. The open ends of the tubes connect the tract to the peritoneal cavity.
The lack of glands explains where lubrication comes from, not how infection reaches the pelvis.
The urethra is a separate opening; it explains bladder infections, not pelvic ones.
Blood vessels in the ligament are not the route; the infection travels along the open lumen of the tract.

why.correct: The vulva is the external genitals: the mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris, vestibule and the greater vestibular glands that open into it. The cervix and fimbriae are internal.
options: Correct. The labia minora enclose the vestibule.
The cervix is the lower end of the uterus, inside the body at the top of the vagina.
Correct. Only its glans is visible, but the clitoris is part of the vulva.
Correct. The fat pad over the pubic bones is part of the vulva.
Correct. These glands sit beside the vaginal opening and release mucus into the vestibule.
The fimbriae are at the ovary end of the uterine tube, deep in the pelvis.

why.correct: The myometrium, a thick layer of smooth muscle, makes up most of the wall. Its contractions cause menstrual cramps and push the baby out in childbirth.
options: Stratified squamous epithelium lines the vagina, not the uterus. The uterine lining is simple columnar.
Dense connective tissue ties the cervix to the pelvic walls but is not the bulk of the wall.
Correct. The myometrium is smooth muscle.
Adipose tissue fills the breast and the labia majora, not the uterine wall.

why.correct: From outside in: the serous perimetrium, the muscular myometrium, then the endometrium, whose basal layer lies against the muscle and whose functional layer faces the cavity.
Estrogen makes the vaginal epithelial cells store glycogen. Glycogen is broken into sugars, which lactobacilli living in the vagina ferment to lactic acid; the acid keeps the pH at about 3.8 to 4.5.
options: The vaginal wall has no glands.
The cervix secretes mucus, not hydrochloric acid, which is made in the stomach.
Correct. Sugars from the epithelium's glycogen are fermented to lactic acid by lactobacilli.
The urethra opens separately in front of the vagina; urine does not set vaginal pH.

why.correct: Estrogen drives glycogen storage in the vaginal epithelium. With less glycogen, lactobacilli make less lactic acid, the pH rises, and other microbes grow more easily.
options: Correct. Less glycogen means less lactic acid and a less acidic vagina.
The vaginal wall has no glands to stop working. Lubrication normally seeps through the wall from blood vessels.
Low estrogen thins the wall rather than thickening its muscle.
The lining thins but stays a nonkeratinized mucosa; it does not turn into keratinized skin.

why.correct: Lactiferous ducts carry milk from the lobes of the mammary gland to openings at the nipple.
options: Suspensory ligaments are bands of connective tissue from the skin to the chest wall; they do not carry milk.
Correct. These tubes running to the nipple are lactiferous ducts.
Areolar glands are small glands on the surface of the areola, not the ducts inside the breast.
Lobules are the clusters of alveoli at the ends of the ducts, not the ducts themselves.

why.correct: The alveoli are small sacs lined by milk-making cells and wrapped in contractile myoepithelial cells. Clusters of them form lobules.
options: Textbooks use this name for widened parts of the ducts near the nipple; either way, milk is not made there.
The areola is the pigmented skin around the nipple.
Correct. Milk is made in the alveoli.
Fat fills the spaces between the lobes and sets breast size, but it makes no milk.

why.correct: The suspensory ligament of the ovary runs from the ovary to the pelvic side wall, and the ovarian vessels and nerves travel inside it.
options: The ovarian ligament ties the ovary to the uterus, not to the pelvic wall.
The round ligament runs from the uterus forward to the groin.
Correct. The suspensory ligament carries the ovary's blood supply.
The uterine tube is not attached to the ovary and carries no ovarian vessels.

why.correct: The labia majora and the scrotum form from the same pair of skin swellings in the embryo.
options: The glans penis matches the glans of the clitoris.
Correct. The scrotum is the male counterpart of the labia majora.
The bulbourethral glands match the greater vestibular glands.
The corpus spongiosum matches the vestibular bulbs.

why.correct: The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands lie beside the lower part of the vaginal opening. A blocked duct fills with mucus and can form a cyst or abscess there.
options: Correct. That position matches a greater vestibular gland.
The urethra opens in the midline in front of the vaginal opening, not at its lower side edge.
The cervical canal is at the top of the vagina, not at its opening.
Lactiferous ducts are in the breast.

why.correct: There is no duct joining the ovary to the uterine tube. The oocyte enters the pelvic cavity and is caught by the fimbriae.
options: This step is right. The oocyte is released from the ovary's surface.
This step is right. The fimbriae and their cilia draw it in.
This is the error. The ovary and tube are not connected.
This step is right. Cilia and muscle waves move it toward the uterus.
This step is right. The trip takes about three to four days.

why.correct: The hymen is a thin fold of mucosa at the vaginal opening. Its shape varies from person to person and with age and estrogen, and its appearance cannot show sexual history.
options: Correct. It is a variable mucosal fold.
It contains no sphincter muscle and does not close the vagina.
The cervix has a mucus-filled canal, not a sealing layer called the hymen.
Lubrication comes from the vaginal wall, the cervix and the greater vestibular glands, not the hymen.

why.correct: Milk made in the alveoli drains through branching ducts into the lactiferous ducts, which open at the nipple.
options: Correct. The lactiferous ducts carry milk to the nipple.
Areolar glands are small separate glands on the areola that release an oily secretion, not milk channels.
Suspensory ligaments are supporting bands of connective tissue, not ducts.
Uterine tubes carry oocytes, not milk.

why.correct: Almost all follicles are resting primordial follicles, and their oocytes have been paused in prophase I of meiosis since before birth. Only the one oocyte about to be released each month moves on to become a secondary oocyte.
options: Oogonia exist only before birth; none remain in an adult ovary.
Only the single oocyte released each month reaches this stage, just before ovulation.
Correct. The resting pool is primary oocytes paused in prophase I.
An ovum forms only after a sperm enters a secondary oocyte, outside the ovary.

why.correct: Primary oocytes enter meiosis I before birth and arrest in prophase I, after crossing over. They stay there until the rise in LH before their ovulation.
options: Metaphase II is the second pause, reached by the secondary oocyte just before ovulation.
Correct. The long arrest is in prophase I.
Anaphase I separates the homologous pairs; it happens only when meiosis I restarts before ovulation.
Telophase II happens only if a sperm enters and meiosis II finishes.

why.correct: A resting primordial follicle becomes primary when its flat cells become cube-shaped granulosa cells, secondary when the granulosa layers multiply and a theca forms, tertiary when an antrum appears, and mature vesicular just before ovulation. After ovulation its cells become the corpus luteum.
Meiosis I in the oocyte divides the cytoplasm unequally. The secondary oocyte keeps nearly all of it, and the first polar body gets one set of chromosomes and very little else. It later breaks down.
options: Granulosa cells nourish the oocyte. The polar body is a product of the oocyte's own division.
Correct. It is the tiny product of the lopsided first division.
The ring of granulosa cells released with the oocyte is follicle tissue, not a polar body.
That scar is the corpus albicans.

why.correct: The released cell is a secondary oocyte paused at metaphase II. Only the entry of a sperm triggers the rest of meiosis II. Without it, the oocyte stays paused and dies within about 12 to 24 hours.
options: Meiosis II finishes only when a sperm enters; there is no ovum without that trigger.
The oocyte cannot return to the ovary; it is carried along the uterine tube and breaks down.
Correct. It stays arrested at metaphase II and dies.
A secondary oocyte does not divide by mitosis.

why.correct: FSH switches on aromatase in granulosa cells, but they cannot make androgens from cholesterol. In the follicle, theca cells stimulated by LH supply those androgens. Adding androgen to the dish replaces the theca cells' contribution.
options: FSH is a protein hormone that signals the cell; it is not a raw material for steroid synthesis.
Correct. This is the two-cell, two-hormone arrangement.
If granulosa cells lacked FSH receptor proteins, FSH would not switch on aromatase and the added androgen would not be converted.
The theca cells make androgens; the granulosa cells make the estradiol, as the experiment shows.

why.correct: A tertiary follicle is defined by fluid-filled gaps between the granulosa cells merging into one space, the antrum.
options: Correct. The antrum marks the tertiary stage.
Cube-shaped granulosa cells first appear in the primary follicle.
Every follicle from the primordial stage on contains a primary oocyte.
A single layer of flat cells is the primordial follicle.

why.correct: FSH is needed for the late stages of follicle growth and for estradiol production by granulosa cells. Blocking it stalls follicles at the tertiary stage, lowers estradiol and prevents ovulation, while the FSH-independent early stages carry on.

variables.name: Growth of tertiary follicles
variables.why: From the tertiary stage on, follicles need FSH to keep growing, so without FSH signaling they stall.

variables.name: Estradiol made by the follicles
variables.why: FSH switches on aromatase in granulosa cells; blocked, they cannot convert theca androgens into estradiol.

variables.name: Number of primordial follicles that start to grow
variables.why: The earliest stages run on signals inside the ovary and do not depend on FSH.

variables.name: Chance of ovulation that month
variables.why: Without a mature follicle, there is no follicle ready to release a secondary oocyte.

why.correct: Oogenesis gives one large gamete plus polar bodies, pauses in prophase I and metaphase II, and its oogonia are gone by birth. Spermatogenesis divides the cytoplasm equally, gives four sperm, and runs on stem cells throughout adult life. Both make haploid gametes.
options: Correct. One secondary oocyte (or ovum) versus four sperm.
Correct. Primary oocytes wait in prophase I from before birth.
Spermatogenesis divides the cytoplasm equally; oogenesis is the one with unequal divisions.
Correct. Oogonia do not survive past birth, while spermatogonia divide throughout adult life.
Both processes are meiosis, so both make haploid gametes.

why.correct: Atresia is the normal fate of more than 99% of follicles. Follicles start growing and then die, before birth, through childhood and each month in adult life, where a whole group grows and all but one die.
options: A period sheds the functional layer of the endometrium, not oocytes from the ovary.
The corpus luteum forms from the cells of one emptied follicle; it does not take up other oocytes.
Correct. Atresia, not ovulation, empties the ovary.
Very few are left in midlife, and they are not released; the supply runs out.

why.correct: The theca forms from the connective tissue around the follicle at the secondary stage, when the granulosa cells have become several layers thick.
options: A primordial follicle has only a single layer of flat cells.
A primary follicle has a single layer of cube-shaped granulosa cells and no theca yet.
Correct. The outer blue-gray ring first appears at the secondary stage.
The corpus albicans is the scar left long after ovulation, not a growing follicle.

why.correct: The first polar body is the small haploid cell made when meiosis I finishes. It gets a set of chromosomes but almost no cytoplasm.
options: The secondary oocyte is the large haploid cell from the same division, which keeps nearly all the cytoplasm.
The oogonium is the diploid stem cell at the top of the chart, before birth.
Correct. This small cell is the first polar body.
The primary oocyte is diploid and has not yet finished meiosis I.
A second polar body forms later: when meiosis II finishes after a sperm enters, or if the first polar body itself divides. The pinned cell comes straight from meiosis I.

why.correct: After the rise in LH, protein-digesting enzymes weaken the follicle wall where it bulges from the ovary, and prostaglandins are needed for that step. Blocking them can delay rupture even when everything before it is normal.
options: Correct. Rupture of the wall depends on prostaglandins.
Meiosis I resumes inside the oocyte in response to LH and does not depend on the wall opening; the question shows a problem with release.
The follicle had already been selected and reached full size.
Her LH rose normally, so the pituitary step was intact.

why.correct: LH turns the leftover follicle cells into the corpus luteum and keeps stimulating them. Without a signal from an embryo, the corpus luteum still dies after about 12 to 14 days.
options: FSH stays low while the corpus luteum is active; its main targets are growing follicles.
Correct. LH supports the corpus luteum.
Follicles that grow after ovulation do not support the corpus luteum; LH does, and no follicle can ovulate while it is active.
Oxytocin acts on smooth muscle of the uterus and breast; it does not support the corpus luteum.

why.correct: The uterine tube does not contract to pull or eject the oocyte from the ovary. The follicle wall weakens and opens, the oocyte oozes out in fluid over a few minutes, and the fimbriae sweep it in.
options: This step is right. The rise in LH triggers ovulation.
This step is right. Meiosis I finishes shortly before release.
This is the error. Release is a slow ooze through a weakened wall, not an ejection by the tube.
This step is right. Protein-digesting enzymes open the wall.
This step is right. The oocyte leaves wrapped in granulosa cells and is swept into the tube.

why.correct: Once the corpus luteum stops working, it shrinks into a small pale scar of dense connective tissue, the corpus albicans ("whitening body").
options: Correct. It is the scar left behind.
That is the corpus luteum, the stage before it.
A follicle that dies without releasing its oocyte undergoes atresia; it does not form a corpus albicans.
That mound is made of granulosa cells inside a mature follicle.

why.correct: Sperm entry triggers meiosis II in the secondary oocyte, giving one large ovum and a second polar body.
options: The oogonium is the stem cell at the start of oogenesis, before the primary oocyte.
Correct. The second division gives the ovum.
A primary follicle is a structure of cells around a primary oocyte, not a product of meiosis II.
The corpus luteum forms in the ovary from follicle cells, not from the oocyte.

why.correct: Every oocyte began meiosis I before birth, so an oocyte released at 43 has been paused for about 43 years. The protein links holding paired chromosomes weaken over that time, which makes nondisjunction more likely when meiosis I finally finishes.
options: No oocytes are made after birth; hers is older, not newer.
Correct. The long pause lets the chromosome links weaken, raising the risk of nondisjunction.
Oocytes always form by meiosis, and no new ones are made in adult ovaries at any age.
Meiosis II finishes only after a sperm enters, in any woman; skipping it is not the explanation.

why.correct: Sustained high estradiol now pushes GnRH and LH up instead of down, and the rising gonadotropins had been driving the follicle to make still more estradiol. A response that strengthens its own stimulus is positive feedback; it ends when the surge turns the follicle's cells toward making progesterone.
options: Negative feedback would make high estradiol lower LH, as it does for most of the cycle, not raise it.
Correct. Estradiol and the gonadotropins drive each other higher until the surge turns the follicle toward progesterone.
The loop runs through hormones: estradiol in the blood, GnRH in the portal system and LH in the blood.
Antagonistic hormones oppose each other's effects; here estradiol and LH reinforce each other.

why.correct: Estradiol from the dominant follicle climbs to its peak first; sustained high estradiol then triggers the LH surge. Cause comes before effect.
options: The order is reversed: the estradiol peak comes first, and it is what triggers the LH surge.
The curves are offset: estradiol peaks first, then LH.
Correct. The estradiol peak comes before the LH peak.
Estradiol does have a second, smaller hump after ovulation, but its main peak comes before it.

why.correct: Around day 21 the corpus luteum is at its most active, and progesterone is at the peak of its curve.
options: LH is low throughout the luteal phase, held down by progesterone.
Correct. Progesterone from the corpus luteum peaks in the middle of the luteal phase.
FSH is at its lowest in the middle of the luteal phase.
Estradiol has only a smaller second hump then, lower than its peak before ovulation, and it comes from the corpus luteum; no dominant follicle exists in the luteal phase.

why.correct: Progesterone raises resting temperature, and progesterone rises only after ovulation, as the corpus luteum forms. By the time temperature goes up, ovulation has already happened.
options: Correct. Progesterone from the new corpus luteum causes the rise, so it confirms ovulation after the fact.
A temperature rise is a sign that ovulation did happen; cycles without ovulation have no corpus luteum and usually no rise.
The graph shows a rise, lasting until the end of the cycle.
LH itself does not set temperature; the rise follows the progesterone curve, not the LH peak.

why.correct: Sustained high estradiol switches the hypothalamus and pituitary to positive feedback; more GnRH and a more responsive pituitary produce the LH surge. The surge triggers ovulation and turns the follicle's cells into the corpus luteum. Those cells switch from estradiol to progesterone, so estradiol falls and the stimulus for the loop is gone.

The corpus luteum's hormones give strong negative feedback. Progesterone slows GnRH pulses, FSH and LH fall to their lowest levels, and progesterone blocks the LH surge, so no follicle can mature and be released until the corpus luteum dies.
options: Tens of thousands of follicles or more remain in a young woman's ovaries; hormones, not a lack of follicles, are the reason.
Correct. Negative feedback from the corpus luteum keeps the gonadotropins low and prevents an LH surge.
The corpus luteum occupies only the old follicle's site; its effect on other follicles is through hormones.
Oxytocin acts on the uterus and breast, not on follicle growth.

why.correct: The combined pill uses the cycle's own negative feedback. Steady hormones keep GnRH, FSH and LH low, so no follicle dominates, estradiol never rises high enough to switch on positive feedback, and there is no LH surge and no ovulation. The progestin also thickens cervical mucus.

variables.name: GnRH pulse frequency
variables.why: Steady estrogen and progestin keep negative feedback on the hypothalamus all month, and the progestin slows the GnRH pulse generator.

variables.name: LH at mid-cycle
variables.why: Low GnRH and constant negative feedback on the pituitary prevent the LH surge.

variables.name: Estradiol made by her own follicles
variables.why: With FSH held low, no follicle becomes dominant, so the ovaries make little estradiol.

variables.name: Ovulation
variables.why: Without a dominant follicle and without an LH surge, no oocyte is released.

variables.name: Thickness of cervical mucus
variables.why: The progestin keeps the mucus thick and sticky all month, which hinders sperm.

why.correct: Removing the ovaries removes the source of estradiol, progesterone and inhibin. Negative feedback is lost, so the pituitary releases more FSH and LH, as after menopause, and the uterine cycle stops.

variables.name: Blood estradiol
variables.why: The follicles and corpus luteum, the main sources of estradiol, have been removed.

variables.name: Blood inhibin
variables.why: Inhibin comes from granulosa cells and the corpus luteum, which were in the ovaries.

variables.name: Blood FSH
variables.why: With no estradiol or inhibin, negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost, and FSH rises.

variables.name: Blood LH
variables.why: Loss of estradiol and progesterone feedback lets GnRH and LH rise too.

variables.name: Monthly shedding of the functional layer
variables.why: Without the rise and fall of ovarian hormones, the endometrium is not rebuilt and shed each month, so periods stop.

why.correct: The luteal phase is fairly steady at about 14 days, so ovulation comes about 14 days before the next period: 32 − 14 = day 18.
options: Day 14 applies only to a 28-day model cycle.
Day 16 is half of 32. Ovulation is not at the midpoint; it is set by counting back from the next period.
Correct. 32 − 14 = 18.
Day 25 would leave a luteal phase of only about a week, far shorter than the usual 12 to 14 days.

why.correct: The secretory lining depends on progesterone. When the corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls, which sets off inflammation, enzyme breakdown and spasm of the coiled arteries, and the functional layer is shed.
options: The LH surge triggers ovulation, about two weeks before the next shedding.
Rising estradiol rebuilds the lining in the proliferative phase.
FSH rises at about the same time but acts on follicles, not the endometrium.
Correct. Progesterone withdrawal starts menstruation.

why.correct: Progesterone turns the thickened endometrium secretory, raises resting temperature and slows the GnRH pulse generator. Thin mucus and the LH surge are estradiol's effects.
options: Correct. This defines the secretory phase.
Estradiol makes mucus thin and stretchy; progesterone makes it thick.
Correct. Resting temperature is about 0.3 to 0.5 °C higher in the luteal phase.
Correct. This is the basis of its negative feedback.
High, sustained estradiol triggers the LH surge.

why.correct: Low estradiol with low FSH and LH means the ovaries are not being driven. Too little energy for her training slows GnRH pulses, so the pituitary releases little FSH and LH and no follicle matures.
options: If her ovaries had failed, the loss of negative feedback would make FSH and LH high, as after menopause.
A uterine problem would not lower her estradiol, FSH and LH.
Correct. Low gonadotropins with low estradiol point above the ovary, to the hypothalamus.
Her FSH is low, not high.

why.correct: With no follicles left, estradiol and inhibin fall. Loss of their negative feedback lets FSH rise, first and most. A persistently high FSH is the laboratory sign of menopause.
options: Progesterone comes mainly from a corpus luteum, which needs ovulation; it would be low.
Correct. Lost negative feedback raises FSH.
Low FSH would suggest the hypothalamus or pituitary is not driving the ovaries.
Inhibin comes from granulosa cells of growing follicles; with none left, it falls.

why.correct: The pill's hormones are steady, not a sustained high estradiol peak from a dominant follicle. They keep negative feedback on and prevent the LH surge; ovulation does not happen.
options: This step is right. The pill supplies steady hormone levels.
This step is right. Negative feedback keeps the gonadotropins low.
This step is right. Low FSH leaves no follicle to dominate.
This is the error. The pill blocks the LH surge instead of triggering it.
This step is right. Thick mucus is a backup effect.

why.correct: As FSH falls, only the follicle most sensitive to it keeps growing. The dominant follicle has the most FSH receptor proteins, the best blood supply, and granulosa cells that also respond to LH.
options: Correct. Greater sensitivity lets it keep growing on less FSH, and LH receptor proteins give it a second source of support.
FSH comes only from the anterior pituitary.
Every follicle contains an oocyte.
There is no active corpus luteum in the follicular phase; the old one has died.

why.correct: FSH acts on granulosa cells, which surround the oocyte, and on sustentacular (Sertoli) cells, which surround developing sperm. Both are supporting cells that nurture the gametes.
options: Theca cells and interstitial cells are the LH targets; they make androgens.
The corpus luteum depends on LH, and FSH acts on sustentacular cells rather than on spermatids.
Correct. FSH acts on the supporting cells around the gametes in both sexes.
FSH acts on the supporting cells, which then support the gametes.

why.correct: Just before ovulation, estradiol from the dominant follicle is at its peak and progesterone is still low. Estradiol makes cervical mucus thin and stretchy; progesterone later thickens it.
options: That pattern, in the luteal phase, gives thick, sticky mucus.
Correct. Peak estradiol without progesterone gives thin, stretchy mucus.
FSH and LH act on the ovary, not directly on cervical glands.
Inhibin acts on the pituitary, and estradiol is high, not low, at this time.

why.correct: In the last days, the corpus luteum is dying, so its progesterone, estradiol and inhibin fall. With less negative feedback, the pituitary releases more FSH, which rescues the next group of follicles.
options: LH is flat at that time; the next surge comes about two weeks later.
Follicles respond to FSH; they do not make it.
The endometrium is not an FSH source; FSH comes from the anterior pituitary.
Correct. Less negative feedback lets FSH rise.

why.correct: In the first year or two after menarche, estradiol does not yet reliably trigger an LH surge. Many cycles have no ovulation, so their length varies until the positive-feedback system matures.
options: Uterine size does not set cycle length; the ovarian hormones do.
Correct. Irregular early cycles are common while the LH surge mechanism matures.
A 12-year-old has hundreds of thousands of follicles.
Her pituitary makes LH; what is immature is the positive-feedback surge.
